chunks: GPU compute beyond graphics. The question: What are other tasks that GPUs may excel at besides graphics processing? Why?
A GPU helps with any job that applies the same operation to a huge amount of independent data.
The headline example is machine learning, which is mostly multiplying big grids of numbers, called matrices.
Others are scientific simulation, image and video processing, and Monte Carlo methods (averaging many random trials).
A GPU does not help with branchy code, tiny problems, or jobs where copying the data takes longer than the math.
A combine harvester is fantastic on a huge, uniform wheat field. It does the same simple action over and over across a wide area.
It is useless for picking fruit from a few winding orchard trees, where each tree needs a different decision. GPU work is the wheat field.
The harvester also has to be driven to the field first, and that trip counts.
Small matrices are slower on the GPU because launch and transfer dominate.
Past N of about 300 the cubic compute outgrows the quadratic transfer and the speed-up climbs toward the compute ratio (the gray line).
Even at N = 4096 the PCIe copy keeps it near 13x instead of 35x.
Data parallelism: the same operation on many independent data elements. GPGPU: general-purpose computing on a GPU, outside of graphics.
Tensor core: hardware that does a small matrix multiply-add in one operation. Arithmetic intensity: operations done per byte of memory traffic.
Offload: sending a job to the GPU, which adds copying costs ("Offloading work from the CPU").
Multiplying two N times N matrices takes about 2N to the 3 operations on about 12N squared bytes of data (three matrices of 4-byte numbers).
Double N , and the arithmetic grows 8 times, but the data grows only 4 times. So for small N , the copy and launch overhead make the GPU slower.
Past some size the arithmetic outgrows the copying, and the GPU wins. The page's example hardware has a break-even near N equals 300 .
That is the whole idea: the GPU wins when the job is wide, regular and arithmetic-heavy compared with its data.

"GPUs excel at anything that's the same operation over lots of independent data: machine learning, which is mostly matrix multiplies, scientific simulation, image and video processing, FFTs, Monte Carlo and hashing.
The reasons are thousands of parallel threads, regular memory access that uses the wide high-bandwidth memory, and high arithmetic intensity.
They struggle with branchy, serial or pointer-chasing code, small problems, and jobs dominated by PCIe transfers."
